other.title: Plant Medicine Influencer Culture on Social Media
other.abstract:
If plants could speak, who would they elect to spread their message to the world?

In 2020, the rise of social media plant medicine influencers came on the heels of leading cultural figures sharing their psychedelic experiences in popular media, including the New York Times bestselling book, How To Change Your Mind by Michael Pollan, as well as the Netflix documentaries, Have a Good Trip and Fantastic Fungi.

After decades of dormancy tied to the declaration of the “War On Drugs” (1971) and the scheduling of numerous psychedelic compounds under the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, researchers at high-profile institutions like University of New Mexico and Imperial College London renewed clinical investigation of various psychedelics such as DMT and psilocybin in the 1990s and early 2000s, gradually opening the door to a renewed public dialogue around psychedelic compounds and the plants and fungi that harbor them. 

“Social media has democratized access to plant medicine information and education unlike anything in history.”

Coupled with the rise of psychedelic biotech companies like Atai and Compass Pathways and increasing media coverage of the emerging “Psychedelic Renaissance” circa 2020, the taboo around speaking publicly about psychedelics was lifted at the exact moment when influencers around the world were poised to take advantage of their large social media followings across various platforms.…
other.outcome_summary: The article discusses the rise of social media influencers in the plant medicine space, coinciding with increased public interest in psychedelics and renewed clinical research. It highlights how social media has democratized access to information but also risks decontextualizing and commodifying ancient knowledge and psychedelic experiences.

relevance.reason: Discusses social media's role in psychedelic culture and research.
